task: R1 has IPv6 forwarding and addressed interfaces. On the classic IPv6-specific IOS syntax used in this lab, create or enter OSPFv3 process 10.

teaching.hint: Use the IPv6-specific process context named by this platform.
teaching.takeaway: Classic IPv6 OSPF and newer OSPFv3 address-family syntax use different command contexts. Follow the selected platform consistently; creating a process does not activate an interface.

task: This new classic OSPFv3 process runs on an IPv6-only router with no IPv4 interfaces. Set its router ID explicitly to 1.1.1.1 before activation.

teaching.hint: OSPFv3 still needs a 32-bit router identifier.
teaching.takeaway: The dotted-decimal router ID is an identifier, not an IPv4 next hop. Configuring it explicitly avoids relying on IPv4 addresses that this router does not have.

task: You are configuring an operational IPv6 interface. Activate classic OSPFv3 process 10 in area 0 on this interface.

teaching.hint: Classic OSPFv3 enables interfaces directly rather than using IPv4 wildcard network statements.
teaching.takeaway: The process configuration alone does not advertise every LAN. Even a passive client LAN needs interface activation before its prefix can be advertised through other adjacencies.

task: This IPv6 Ethernet link has exactly two routers. Use classic OSPFv3 point-to-point treatment on R1's interface; the peer is configured the same way.

teaching.hint: The OSPF network type controls whether this link needs a DR/BDR.
teaching.takeaway: Point-to-point operation removes the DR/BDR election without changing Ethernet itself. Check for the expected Full adjacency and consistent interface settings on both ends.

task: On a shared broadcast LAN, make this R1 interface ineligible for OSPFv3 DR/BDR using classic IPv6 syntax.

teaching.hint: The eligibility rule transfers from OSPFv2, but this interface command is IPv6-specific.
teaching.takeaway: Priority 0 prevents election on this interface. OSPFv3 compares router IDs for eligible ties, not the numerically largest global IPv6 address.

task: Gi0/2 already participates in this classic OSPFv3 process but connects only client PCs. Suppress Hellos and neighbor formation there while retaining its advertised prefix.

teaching.hint: Stop neighbor formation without removing the interface's process activation.
teaching.takeaway: Passive treatment is appropriate for a client-only LAN. Removing OSPF activation instead would withdraw its advertised prefix, even while transit neighbors stayed Full.

task: On R1 using classic IPv6 OSPF syntax, display the OSPFv3 neighbor IDs, adjacency states and local interfaces.

teaching.hint: Select the IPv6 OSPF neighbor display, not the generic IPv6 neighbor cache.
teaching.takeaway: The OSPF router ID differs from the neighbor's link-local forwarding address. A repeated ID on two rows can describe the same router across two different local links.

task: Using classic IPv6 OSPF syntax, inspect GigabitEthernet0/0 for its process, area, network type, effective timers and link-local neighbor context.

teaching.hint: Detailed OSPF interface evidence narrows a missing adjacency beyond basic IP address state.
teaching.takeaway: Compare area, instance, timers, passive status and usable link-local communication with the peer. Matching global prefixes alone does not establish a working OSPFv3 adjacency.

task: R1's OSPFv3 neighbors are established. Display the IPv6 prefixes currently installed from OSPF, including their scoped next hops.

teaching.hint: A synchronized neighbor does not prove that the remote client LAN participates.
teaching.takeaway: Read the global destination prefix separately from the link-local next hop and exit interface. Verify the reverse client prefix too before treating a working adjacency as end-to-end connectivity.
